summary:
Nunavut stands under Canada's national framework, and layers its own statutory protection on top of it. In March 2017 the Legislative Assembly voted unanimously on third reading of Bill 31, amending the territory's Human Rights Act to add gender identity and gender expression alongside sexual orientation as prohibited grounds of discrimination. Justice Minister Keith Peterson said the amendment would make clear that discrimination against transgender people is prohibited; at the time Nunavut was the first Canadian territory to list these grounds, with nine provinces and one territory already doing so.

Nunavut's birth certificates carry a non-binary option. On 18 September 2025, Members of the Legislative Assembly voted 12-8 in committee of the whole to restore a third non-binary sex-designation on Nunavut birth certificates through amendments to the Vital Statistics Act, after the standing committee had struck the provision from Health Minister John Main's May 2025 bill. The bill then passed third reading, and sponsor Adam Arreak Lightstone stated that the Government of Nunavut now joins the rest of Canada in recognizing non-binary and transgender individuals.

The territorial government funds gender-affirming care. Reporting from 22 March 2022 states that Nunavut's Health Department began funding transition-related care for transgender and non-binary residents, with breast augmentation, chest contouring, hysterectomy and vaginoplasty named among covered procedures, under a partnership with the Metropolitan Centre of Surgery in Montreal. The local LGBTQ group Positive Space called the funding overdue while flagging information gaps for residents living outside Iqaluit.

Nationally, police-reported hate crime targeting gender identity and expression rose 8% to 139 incidents in 2024, a fourth consecutive annual increase and a 184% rise since 2020, according to a Statistics Canada release published 30 March 2026. Sexual-orientation-motivated incidents fell 26% to 658. Hate-crime rates run roughly 2.5 times higher in metropolitan areas than in smaller towns, a gap relevant to Nunavut, which has no metropolitan reporting hub of that scale. Egale Canada's analysis of the same police-reported data supplies national 2SLGBTQ+ victimisation context rather than territorial figures.
tangentialFactors:
Nunavut's protections rest on two layers: the federal regime under the Canadian Human Rights Act and the Criminal Code's hate-motivation provisions, and the territorial Human Rights Act as amended in 2017. A visitor in Nunavut can invoke either layer when facing discrimination in employment, housing or accommodation.

The 2025 Vital Statistics Act amendment places Nunavut alongside the other provinces and territories in offering a non-binary marker on birth certificates, a document rule that bears on how a gender-nonconforming visitor's local documents might be read if they need territorial records issued.

Sub-national turbulence elsewhere in Canada, including Saskatchewan's 2023 Education (Parents' Bill of Rights) Amendment Act and Alberta's 2024 health, education and sport statutes shielded by Bill 9 in 2025, has no counterpart in Nunavut's own legislative record; the territorial pattern runs the other way, toward expanded recognition.
localsOnly:
Nunavut residents can file discrimination complaints under the territorial Human Rights Act, which since 2017 expressly names gender identity and gender expression as protected grounds alongside sexual orientation.

Residents seeking gender-affirming surgery can access territorially funded care through the Health Department's partnership with the Metropolitan Centre of Surgery in Montreal, though the local group Positive Space has flagged that residents outside the capital face information gaps about the programme.

Residents can obtain a birth certificate with a non-binary sex designation under the Vital Statistics Act as amended in September 2025.
outOfScopeNotes:
Nunavut-specific hate-crime volumes are not established by the Statistics Canada release, which reports national totals and does not break out territorial figures for gender identity or expression motivations; the metropolitan-versus-smaller-town rate gap is a national pattern whose application to Nunavut's communities is inferred, not sourced.

No Nunavut-specific incident of violence against a trans person, and no territorial correctional-facility placement dispute, appears in the inventory; conditions of detention in Nunavut's own institutions are unresolved on this record.

Egale Canada's 2024 analysis supplies national context only; its findings are not territorial data for Nunavut.
